utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. After the break we had yesterday, I bid good morning to all persons present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the representatives of the accused, the accused, and all the staff of this courtroom. Today we have two witnesses planned. There appears there may be a problem with one of the two witnesses. But before addressing the problem of witnesses, there are two points to regulate. First of all, the Chamber notes with satisfaction the presence of the famous model that we have in front of us, which will allow the witnesses coming to indicate the places, as marked by the small cards. So it will be easier to find the various localities. From the position of the Chamber, we can see white and green. We assume that the green are wooded areas and the green areas, but certainly we will be given additional explanations. In any event, this model will be very useful for all of us. A second point that I wish to address has to do with the question of documents which the Prosecution wishes to tender into evidence. The Prosecution drew up a table, and the Chamber received yesterday the comments of the Defence regarding those documents. I spent a part of the afternoon looking at this table and making calculations regarding the documents admitted and those contested. According to me, there are 212 documents that are not contested and 655 that are. So we have a hard core of more than 200 documents which have not provoked any objections on the part of the Defence. These documents, therefore, are referred to in the table which has been attached by the Defence to its written submissions. The Defence in its brief indicates that it contests documents principally for two reasons: First, on the grounds of relevance; and also, contesting the authenticity of documents, either because of the quality of the signatures or various other reasons. So these are the two grounds on the basis of which a certain number of documents are challenged -- not a certain number, but 655 documents, which means that these documents will be produced by the Prosecution through future witnesses and that then the Defence counsel will object to them on the grounds of relevance or authenticity. So we need to regulate the fate of 212 documents. You had your administrative meeting yesterday in this connection, and one of the solutions envisaged would be for the Chamber to render a decision in writing regarding these 212 noncontested documents. This can be done. We will discuss it amongst ourselves during the break. But the problem that could arise is the following, and that is that these documents are documents that we haven't seen and that we do not know the contents of. The Prosecution has disclosed them to the Defence, who of course studied them, but we don't have them. It would appear that the Prosecution is producing copies of those documents now. Will we have those documents before the date envisaged in April, that is, next week? We, of course, are not requesting all of the documents, but we could have at least the 212 noncontested documents. Because the Chamber will have two possibilities - but we are going to discuss it - and that is if we don't receive those documents from now until the date envisaged, they can be marked for identification, which will be transformed into an exhibit number when we get the documents; or a second solution would be that we trust both parties regarding their relevance and then our decision will mean that they will be given a final number. But before we deliberate amongst ourselves, I should like to hear the position of the Prosecution regarding the copying of these documents and when the Chamber may gain possession of them and have them in binders. Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in respect as to when the Prosecution will make available the documents which are not contested, it was the understanding of the Prosecution to date that we would produce such documents on the 8th of April. It's the understanding of the Prosecution that based on a decision of the Trial Chamber, what has been the suggestion of the parties in the course of the yesterday evening's meeting, following a proposal by the registrar, that then the P numbers would be given to the documents and afterwards, namely on the 8th of April, the Prosecution produces nine or ten binders of such documents containing the noncontested ones. It's a huge effort for the Prosecution to put together the binders, and the Prosecution will most likely outsource this work. Therefore, the Prosecution, as the Defence as well, would very much appreciate if the Chamber could render its decision in the course of this week. It's the view of the Prosecution - and obviously it's the view of the Defence as well, since they did not contest such documents - that these documents are relevant to the current proceedings. Therefore, it's the suggestion of the Prosecution that once the Chamber has made its decision detailing the P numbers, the Prosecution will take care of putting together the respective numbers of binders and will hand these binders over and will tender these documents on the 8th of April. If I may address a second issue you, Mr. Presiding Judge, have briefly talked about. Defence in their yesterday's submission has shown and has indicated that they for a number of reasons - namely, authenticity or relevancy - do contest the majority of the documents. The Prosecution would like to address the Defence concerns and their challenges; however, it would be very beneficial if Defence could enlighten both the Chamber and the Prosecution in respect to each document, what the challenge is about, since only then the Prosecution has a position to actually address the concerns of the Defence. This may have an impact on the Prosecution calling certain witnesses. If the relevancy is challenged, this is more or less a pure legal issue. If, however, the authenticity or the chain of custody is challenged, the Prosecution would need to call certain witnesses. Therefore, the Prosecution would very much appreciate if the Defence could inform both the Chamber and the Prosecution in respect to each and every document what their challenges are about. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to the Defence, but just a small point so that there should be no misunderstanding. Originally, the Chamber indicated that the 8th of April would be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the date when the documents would be officially admitted. At the time - and you can refer to the transcript - it was indicated that we would spend that day of the 8th of April in giving numbers to the 92 bis testimony and also giving numbers to documents, having stated at the time that we would have those documents in our hands. And as indicated at the time, Mr. Registrar would give them a number document by document. Subsequently to what was said then, the Defence and the Prosecution, who thought the matter over, suggested that they meet with the legal officer so as to envisage a different procedure which would enable time to be saved. And it is within the context of this new procedure that it was suggested that the Chamber make a written ruling on the admission of documents. So that is the problem as I wish to recall. If we order the admission of those documents, there's a risk of us taking a decision prior to the 8th of April without having the documents. The Prosecution tells us that there will be nine binders by the 8th of April and not ten, so I don't know why there are -- there's one on standby, but there must be a reason. We are told that these documents will be put in binders, but there are only two methods of doing it: Either the method following the numbers, binder number 1 covering exhibit numbers appearing in the Annex, and then one can find one's way; or another, more elaborate form of classification, which would be to put the documents in relation to the offences or the locations. But that would be rather more difficult. But it is up to the Prosecution to decide, of course, though there are several methods of proceeding in this classification of documents. But we will render a decision on what is to be done. The Prosecution has raised an important problem, and that is that there are 655 contested documents. The Defence teams, could they tell us at this stage why they are contested in rough terms? I gather that it is either on the basis of relevance or authenticity. But as the Prosecution has indicated, if documents are contested on the basis of relevance, that can cause graver problems than those contested on the basis of authenticity. I now turn to the Defence to hear their point of view regarding the documents. On the 29th of March -- their brief is dated the 29th of March, but it is rather brief. It's only a page and a half. Mr. Bourgon, as I know that you were working on this submission, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam Judge. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. President. The position of the Defence, Mr. President, was expressed in the document that we filed yesterday on behalf of the Defence for the two accused. Our objective in filing this document was to follow up on the decision of the Chamber. The difficulty that we faced was that the documents for which the Defence was able to agree to, even before the documents were presented to the Chamber, those were the documents on which we agreed regarding admissibility. You mentioned the figure of 212; the figure that I have was a bit higher, but I don't think it is a significant matter for this morning. What is important to note is that regarding the other documents, whose either authenticity or relevance we contest, we're of the opinion that for those documents to be admitted there must be a certain discussion before the Chamber document by document, as the Chamber had indicated. The documents which are mentioned in our response filed yesterday are documents which can be admitted without even having a debate about them. Regarding those documents, to facilitate the proceedings we suggest that the Chamber could give them a number for identification, which would allow the Prosecution to produce the binders, as we discussed yesterday, and then simply the ID would be removed and all those documents can be admitted en bloc, which would be a sound basis for these proceedings. The question of marking for identification was not discussed yesterday, but in view of what the Chamber has said this morning, this would be a way of avoiding all problems: A decision by the Chamber with numbers for identification; the Prosecution produces the documents and then the whole set of documents is admitted and the identification removed. As for the other documents, we as the Defence are ready to proceed in two ways, either case by case, witness by witness in the course of the trial, and then at the end of the trial the documents which were not admitted can be the object of a debate. Or, if the Prosecution and the Chamber prefers, we could have a discussion document by document before that. We simply thought, Mr. President, to convey our observations document by document in writing would not be productive at this stage. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon, for your remarks. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Firstly, Your Honours, we fully appreciate that Your Honours do have to have the documents before you before they can be admitted in order that they are considered by Your Honours before a formal decision is made. And as Mr. Bourgon said - and I'm sure my learned friends from the Prosecution would be able to do this - a copy can be provided with identification numbers before admission. Secondly, on the question of the documents that are challenged, Your Honours, what would be most helpful for us is if the Prosecution could indicate - which is a normal procedure in many jurisdictions - could indicate which witnesses relate to which documents, which witnesses they envisage would introduce the documents. Because part of the problem we face when considering a number of these documents is we can't fully appreciate relevancy because we are not sure which witness is going to comment on the document. And likewise, authenticity; if the source of the document is uncertain, then we have challenged it because we're not sure which witness would in fact be able to indicate that the document does exist and is a document that was properly prepared. So that would be a first step, from our part, is if the Prosecution could indicate which witnesses may be able to comment on those documents. And then we could consider whether or not it was possible at that stage to perhaps narrow the number of documents further. I would suggest, Your Honour, that this is an ongoing process and perhaps we could keep working with the Prosecution on this, to see whether it was possible to reach a solution before we brought it before Your Honours again. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. The problem that we now face is as follows: We have hundreds of documents which will be admitted through witnesses who will be called to give their testimony. It would be very useful if, based on the tables that were made by the Prosecution and the Defence which indicate one document by another -- which witnesses will be talking about which documents. This is a good indicator which will allow both the Prosecution and the Defence as well as the Chamber to have a much clearer picture of all that. In addition to that, it may be useful, but it is up to the Prosecution to give it a thought - it is based on my experience that I am telling you this - with regard to the duties that you perform - and I myself have performed various duties - that's why I'm telling you that it would be very useful to mention if there is a reference to either the indictment or the pre-trial procedure, to mention that. It would -- this would be useful for all of us. This applies to the Defence at the time when they start presenting their evidence. So this remark applies to all of us. It would help all of us to get our bearings. Since we have now heard the position of the Defence, and they are faced with hundreds of documents that have to be admitted through witnesses, and according to the Defence they wish to have at least an indication as to what witnesses will be tied to certain documents. Mr. Withopf, the Trial Chamber has still not rendered a decision. We are going to discuss before we decide. But based on what you have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. heard, is there anything you wish to add? The discussion has enabled us to seize the problem and to try and find the best possible solution. Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There are a number of areas the Prosecution would like to touch upon. The Prosecution would prefer, as earlier on in the proceedings indicated by the Trial Chamber, that there is a discussion about the contested documents, followed by a decision of the Trial Chamber. Such proceedings would certainly accelerate the trial proceedings, taking into account that the Prosecution envisages to have about 25 more witnesses in these proceedings which will appear live in court. What means by 625 or so documents, the Prosecution would have to tender more than 20 to 30 documents via each one of the witnesses, which would certainly have a serious impact on the speed of the proceedings. For that reason only but also for a number of additional reasons, it appears to be more efficient to have a discussion document by document, even if it takes a full day, and then to get the Trial Chamber's decision in respect to the admissibility of such documents. In respect to the context, Mr. President, Your Honours, Defence has always taken a very broad view what the context, the historical and political and military and economical context, should be about and to what extent it should be discussed and considered in the course of these proceedings. Therefore, the Prosecution at this point in time, without having got additional information by the Defence, to some extent does not understand why the Defence is contesting such a high number of documents. The Prosecution also wishes to draw the attention of Your Honours to the fact that amongst the many contested documents there is an extremely high number of documents which are official documents, and the Trial Chamber repeatedly has expressed its views that such official documents, with stamps and signatures stemming from whatever state authorities, should be admitted into evidence. There are a number of orders by the accused Kubura which are contested. These are just examples that show why the Prosecution is, at this point in time, without additional information from the Defence side, not in a position to address the challenges of the Defence. I'm referring in that respect to numbers 227 to 229 on the Defence list. There are certainly far more. This is just an example. In respect to the wish of the Trial Chamber that they want to have a copy of all documents which are not contested in order to allow them to make an informed decision once the Prosecution wishes to tender these documents, the Prosecution is certainly able to produce such a binder prior to 8 of April for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. That shouldn't be too much of a problem. Otherwise, the Prosecution is in agreement with the Defence in respect to the tendering of the noncontested documents. The decision of the Trial Chamber could identify the ID - marked for identification - numbers and then on the 8th of April these documents should be given a final exhibit number. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Let me summarise. The position of both parties is as follows: The Defence has just told us that they contest a number of documents. They wish those documents to be tendered through witnesses. As for the other documents which have not been admitted through witnesses, the Defence proposes that there should be a special conference about these documents. As for the Prosecution, they have a view somewhat different to the Defence; they want a conference to be organised about the contested documents and then call the witnesses, in order to gain time. With regard to this proposal for a meeting that would deal with the contested documents, I believe that such a meeting would take several days because a certain number of documents are likely to be contested by the Defence, in which case there will be a discussion between the Defence and the Prosecution. The Judges will have the last say in that, but this may take a few days. This is a problem that we are facing. For example, on the list of the documents that we have - and this document originates from Serif Patkovic, the list of officers of the 7th Muslim Brigade - this is an official document, however it has been contested. I believe that it hasn't been contested because of the names of the officers but because of its relevancy. If the list of the officers is what is being contested, then it will take some more time. This list could also be admitted through a witness. This is just an example of problems which may arise. Bearing in mind the proposal put forward by the Prosecution, which is that there would be a meeting to discuss documents, what has the Defence to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, the Defence would like to give a few clarifications with regard to the documents that have not been contested. All the documents that are official documents, all the documents that originate from the government or which are enactments issued by the parliament have been accepted by the Defence. At the same time, the documents that originate from international organisations, such as the European Community Monitoring Mission or the United Nations Protection Forces, all of these documents are also something that the Defence can accept. We have a problem, however, with regard to all the other documents. I believe that it would be useful for me to give you an example with regard to the admissibility of documents based on the signature, documents that originate from the 3rd Corps which have been signed by General Hadzihasanovic. When we recognise General Hadzihasanovic's signature, we accept such a document. However, if we were faced with the document originating from the 3rd Corps and if we didn't recognise the signature, if we were aware of the procedure that led to this document, and if we know that the document was signed not by the accused but by somebody else, we will again accept this document. As for the documents that we contest with regard to their admissibility, those documents are the ones for which we cannot establish what was the procedure according to which those documents were drafted. Those documents are the ones which do not originate from the 3rd Corps, but those are the documents which may have been exchanged among the brigades within the 3rd Corps, for example, the 306th Brigade. This is not only about the 7th Muslim Brigade but also the two brigades within the 3rd Corps. It is very difficult for the Defence to voice their opinion about the admissibility of such documents without some prior information. As my colleague Dixon has already said, as for the relevancy of the documents, if the Defence is aware of the link between the document and the indictment, it would be much easier for us to examine such a document in the light of the indictment and to be aware of how the Prosecution wants to use this document. As for the proposal put forward by the Prosecution, we believe that discussing each and every document may take time, may last several days. It would be a long process in order for us to look at the document. So it is quite possible that it might take several days. However, if the Trial Chamber has to render a decision on the procedure, Mr. President, we would like to establish a link between the indictment and the witness who might assist us in establishing the relevancy of such a document with regard to the indictment. Maybe it would be best for us to introduce documents through witnesses who come to give testimony before this Trial Chamber. That's how we would be certain that all the oral evidence has been heard, and it would be much better at that moment to establish the relevance of every document. And finally, with regard to the context, it is true that from the very beginning of this procedure the Defence has tried to establish the relevance of the context. We have explained that in several written submissions, and we believe that the context is very important to understanding the legal significance of some of the admitted documents. The context is important because it played a direct role and it had a bearing on the capacity of the accused in performing his duties of commander. However, Mr. President, when the Prosecution speaks about the context it is very important for them as well, because it doesn't have the same relevance with regard to the duties. The context has to be put in the perspective of the counts of the indictment. When the Defence mentions the context, we imply the conditions under which the accused perform his duties. In both cases it is the same context; however, the goal of presenting it to the Trial Chamber is not the same. I would like to give one more clarification at the end, and this refers to the chain of custody of the documents. It is very important to say, Mr. President, that most of the documents which we contest originate from the collection called the collection of documents on Sarajevo, which was taken from the archives of the government in Sarajevo. The process should be explained before the Trial Chamber. The documents were first taken from Sarajevo. They were transferred through the -- to the Tribunal. This was done by the OTP. When we arrived in Sarajevo in order to request some documents, there were none left, and this is when we started negotiating with the Prosecution in order to find out where the documents are, how they can be returned to Sarajevo so as to enable us to have access to them over there. The OTP have given us documents either on CD-ROM, on the electronic media. We don't have any doubts about the procedure. We are just talking about several stages of the procedure: First, the documents were classified in Sarajevo. Then they were transferred to the Office of the Prosecutor. They were then put on the electronic media and given to the Defence. There are some documents which are questionable and which require some additional information. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, I'm going to give you the floor, but before that Mr. Dixon wanted the floor. Mr. Dixon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Our position would be that at this stage it is too soon to look to have a discussion in the courtroom about each and every document. Our proposal would be that, rather, what we do is now that the Prosecution is on notice about the documents that we contest or the ones that we have a question mark over, that they proceed on that basis with the rest of the presentation of their case, seeking to introduce the documents that they wish to rely upon through the witnesses that are still to come, and there may be more witnesses as well, and that at the end or towards the end of the Prosecution case the situation can be reassessed. Your Honours, in our submission, it would be very difficult to discuss these documents in abstract. They have to be looked at in relation to the evidence. And perhaps at the end of the case we'll then have a better idea of what documents are still contested or are still outstanding. And then the matter could be reconsidered again before Your Honours. What I said earlier on may still be of application in that we could, between the Prosecution and the Defence, as the witnesses are to come, keep our discussions open and keep meeting with the Prosecution to try and see what are the real issues that are contested so as to focus the evidence that the witnesses might need to give. And only at a later stage, then, bring it back before Your Honours again. There is one other matter which I should emphasise in relation to why some of the documents are contested, and that applies particularly for Mr. Kubura, and that is that many of the documents, including some of the orders that were mentioned by my learned friend, are not orders that were issued, it appears, during the time of the indictment. And they are either orders that were issued before the time of the indictment or much later. Your Honours will be aware that the Prosecution on many occasions has contested documents the Defence has sought to introduce because they've been outside the time frame of the indictment, and we have made a similar objection. But it might be when -- when a witness is called that that document can be shown to be relevant in some way, and in that procedure, with the witness here, we can then resolve the matter. So our suggestion would be we should continue with the Prosecution case. They are on notice of what are the documents that are contested. And they can now adjust their case accordingly. And so that extent this process, in our view, has been extremely helpful. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Withopf. And at 10.00 we are going to bring the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Withopf has mentioned 25 witnesses. Can you please tell us whether these are witnesses that will start arriving today, or are these additional witnesses with regard to the schedule that we have received for the months of April and May? The 25 witnesses that you have mentioned, are they on top of the list or are they already on the list that we have received? Can you please clarify. You have the floor, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the 25 witnesses - and I actually wish to emphasise that these are about 25 witnesses, there may be a few more or even a few less - are the witnesses which the Prosecution has already detailed in its recent submission detailing the order of the witnesses the Prosecution will call in April and in May. There are obviously a few additional witnesses, so the total number will figure between 25 and 30, maybe even less. If I may please address a number of issues which have been raised by our learned friends from the Defence side. Even if one would proceed following the suggestion by the Defence to tender documents through witnesses, it would still be very helpful for the Prosecution to know for what reasons certain documents are contested, since it makes a difference whether a document is contested because if -- because it's alleged non-relevance or because of its -- or because of issues of authenticity. Again, even if one wishes to proceed along the lines Defence has suggested, it would still be extremely helpful and it would accelerate proceedings if Defence could inform us in more concrete detail about their concerns. The Prosecution not necessarily does share the concerns of the Defence that a discussion in court about the contested documents would last for days, since it can be anticipated that issues related to the relevance of documents can be decided upon en bloc, since relevance issues, as we have seen in the past, can be treated in certain categories and such categories would certainly enable the Trial Chamber to render its decision on short notice, if necessary. My learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence has addressed the Sarajevo collection. The Sarajevo collection is an issue which has been discussed over the last two and a half years on all -- basically on all Rule 65 ter Conferences and Status Conferences. There is a full record of all issues surrounding the Sarajevo collection on the official court records. The Prosecution would be in a position, if needed, to present evidence in respect to the chain of custody, in respect to all documents that stem from the Sarajevo collection. Actually, we have the impression that most of the documents which are contested by the Defence actually do stem from this collection. This, for the information of the Trial Chamber, is a collection of about 50.000 pages of documents which was seized in October 2000 by the Prosecution from the ABiH main archive in Sarajevo. These are all official documents. Orders, reports - and this addresses a further issue raised by my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence - orders which were not issued by either of the accused but were reported between different units, such as orders and other reports are usually, as Defence is very well aware of, are usually copied to the 3rd Corps command, what would imply that the accused Hadzihasanovic became certainly aware of such materials. The Prosecution in its pre-trial brief extensively in the many footnotes has indicated to both the Defence and the Trial Chamber which documents relate to which portions of the indictment, and it's also pretty easy by carefully reading the pre-trial brief and the references made in the pre-trial brief to the documents to identify which documents relate to which charges. The Prosecution - and this is to address the very last proposal made by our learned colleagues from the Defence side - is a bit hesitant to follow a suggestion that the parties discuss all related issues to the admissibility of contested documents amongst themselves for the only reason that the Prosecution -- and I really wish to remind both the Chamber and the Defence to the fact that there was a huge debate at the beginning of these proceedings, Mr. President, Your Honours, about stipulations. At some point in time we were told by the Defence, "We will come back to the Prosecution and we will discuss it." At no point in time Defence came back to the Prosecution. For that only reason, the Prosecution is extremely hesitant to leave this issue of the admissibility of the contested documents for the parties alone to somehow discuss it and at the very end of the proceedings to make the Chamber -- or to put the Chamber in a position to make a decision. Therefore, the Prosecution continues to suggest that these issues are discussed in one of the court sessions in the near future. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will deliberate amongst ourselves, and we will convey to you our final position regarding this issue as quickly as possible so that you should know. Everyone understands that the objective sought by everyone is to avoid wasting time uselessly and to have proceedings which will certainly establish the truth and allow for an adversarial debate, because that is one of our main principles. So we will deliberate amongst ourselves and then let you know what our final position is. It is a good idea for everyone to be able to express their point of view, which will allow us to make an enlightened decision in the light of your observations. Mr. Withopf, I understand that one of the two witnesses has been withdrawn. Could you inform us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, for this purpose, could we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before the witness arrives, the Defence would simply like to indicate that we would like to address the Chamber regarding the witnesses planned for next week, because -- in view of the communications between the two parties regarding documents of the Monitoring Mission of the European Union. That will be addressed next week. So we would like to address the Chamber on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be best if you do that straight away. That is simpler.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. So briefly, the situation has to do with the documents coming from the Monitoring Mission. We had some exchanges with the Prosecution on this point. We are aware of all the efforts that have been made by the Prosecution to give us access to those documents. According to the latest available information, as discussed yesterday evening, the Prosecution should be or could be in a position to provide us today with the list of documents which it has in its possession so that we might tell them which documents are missing. According to the numbers given to us, the Prosecution has about 3.500 documents in its possession originating from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, 3.500 documents in all, in different categories. When we have the list, we will immediately and as quickly as possible look through them to identify those that are missing, that we didn't obtain. Either they were not used by the Prosecution since the beginning of the trial or which we did not obtain from the archives in Sarajevo. We believe that in the best of cases the response to this question will affect a number between 500 and 1.000 documents that we did not receive. We will communicate this result to the Prosecution as quickly as possible, in the best of cases on Friday morning. Then the Prosecution should once again contact the Mission in Sarajevo, as well as one of the governments that gave these documents to the Prosecution. And once they get a reply, then we will be provided with those documents. In the best of cases, we will not be able to have those documents before the end of business on Monday or Tuesday. And the witness planned for next Tuesday is a witness coming from the European Union Monitoring Mission in Central Bosnia. For this reason, we have conveyed to the Prosecution that we would like to have a minimum of two days between the day when we receive the documents and the time when the first Monitoring Mission witness appears before this Chamber. If we receive the documents on Monday, the Prosecution would not be able to proceed with that witness before Wednesday or even Thursday, the 8th of April, which could be a problem. The Prosecution has suggested that we have the examination-in-chief next week and then the cross-examination could take place later, once we familiarise ourselves with those documents. I think it is important to highlight the situation to Your Honours. We are discussing the matter with the Prosecution. We have suggested that they change the order of witnesses. Apparently they have difficulties in doing that, but my learned friend will explain that for you. For us the point is that we should receive the documents at least two days prior to the hearing of that particular witness of the European Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before continuing, Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me first check whether you hear the interpretation of my words into your own language. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You have been called by the Prosecution to give your testimony in court, and within this testimony I have to ask you to take the solemn declaration. In order to do that, you first have to identify yourself. Can you please give us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hakan Birger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm birthed in Sweden. The place is Tomelilla, and it was the 26th of August, 1955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a lieutenant colonel in the Swedish Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what were your duties in Central Bosnia? What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was company commander in the 1st Nordic Battalion in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before a court, either before an international court or before a national court? Have you ever given your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the first time that you give a testimony. You have to take the solemn declaration, so can you please read the text that you are going to be given by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief, I have to give you some information about the way your testimony is going to take place. You are a Prosecution witness. You are going to testify about the facts that you witnessed in 1993. You're going to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution. Try as much as possible to give complete answers, because we don't have any written documents and the only thing that counts is what you are going to tell us, because the procedure before this Tribunal is oral. And to that effect, the Prosecution is going to ask you questions. Once they are finished with the examination-in-chief, the Defence counsel representing the accused, who are seated on your left, will also put some questions to you within the scope of the cross-examination. They're going to ask you questions in order to verify your credibility and also in order to clarify the context within which the events that you witnessed developed, and also they are going to put questions to you to corroborate the Defence case. The Defence are going to ask you precise questions. Can you please answer in the same way. If at any point in time you think that the question is too complicated, the person who has put it to you may be asked to rephrase it. Don't hesitate to ask the person who has put a question to you to rephrase it. When a question is complex, take your time before you answer. Since it's been ten years since the events that you are testifying about, and if you can't remember the facts, you may say so. That is also going to provide you with -- provide us with a precise answer. The three Judges, who are seated in front of you, may also put questions to you should they deem necessary to do so. The Judges may ask you technical questions about your military career. The Judges can also interrupt either the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination in order to ask questions whenever they need clarification. If at any time the Judges believe that there is something that needs to be clarified, they may interrupt the questions and ask -- and put questions to you. You have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, which means that you are not supposed to give false testimony. False testimony may expose the witness to a penalty. And there's also another situation in which a witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate him, which means that at that moment the witness may refuse to answer. It arises from the common law that a person cannot testify against themselves. It is then up to the Chamber to compel the witness to answer the question. The witness will then answer. However, the testimony compelled in this way cannot be used as evidence against the witness. So in general terms, this is how this Tribunal functions, and this is how this procedure develops. Since this is the first time you are giving your testimony, I just wanted to help you to get your bearings, and that's why I have given you the clarifications. In front of you you see a model. Maybe during the testimony that you are going to give you are going to be asked to find certain locations. Without further ado, I'm turning to the Prosecution and I'm giving them the floor for their examination-in-chief. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I add my greetings to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you briefly describe your military career, starting from the earliest time when you donned a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I started with my conscript 1972, 1973. After that, I was starting -- studying for a military career and in 1981, I was an officer. And I belonged to a mechanised brigade. That means both infantry and tank in the brigade. And I was more or less an infantry. And to the time of 1992, 1993 - sorry - I was battalion commander in the brigade and -- yeah. That's my background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber that in 1993 you were in Bosnia. When did you first go to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: In the middle of September 1993, I was -- belonged to a racket team for one week. We started in Sarajevo airport, and with APCs up to Kiseljak, Vares, Tuzla. And then after this week we went back again to Scandinavia, to Denmark, to train together with Danish part in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber how it came about that you were involved in this mission to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Well, first I have looked a lot in the television what's going on down in Bosnia, and I don't like what I can see there, what is happening with the civilians and the children and so on. So I said to myself, "Somebody better do anything about it." And in the spring 1993, the Swedish government decided to be ready with a battalion, not to take part, to get down there, but to be ready. The battalion commander couldn't handle it, so he asked me to be one of the company commanders. What I say before, what I have seen on the television and the news and so on, and I know him very well and I like his leadership. And he -- we have the same opinion about how we should use mechanised units and so on. So it was very easy to said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that point in time in the spring of 1993 and, in fact, throughout 1993, what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I was major in the Swedish Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When in fact did your company deploy to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I was down there in the last September with my platoon leaders. We were about eight or ten soldiers in my company. We arrived to Tuzla this day, and the next day, the 1st of October, we used our vehicles and got down to Vares, and where we lived together with a Canadian engineer company to somewhere outside Vares. And my first soldiers arrived the 20th of October. And after this they came day to day, but they were also delayed from -- because they were in Pancevo in Serbia and it was not so easy for the unit to fly into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what year are these events that we're talking about taking place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain why your soldiers were delayed in Pancevo, in Serbia, what they were doing there.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The first, we don't take down the whole battalion in the same day, but the plan for that, we train from Denmark, so it takes time; we have a lot of equipment, vehicles, and so on. And the second was that they have to wait because there was some problem with the train to go from Pancevo to the border of Bosnia. And I don't know, maybe it was something from -- to stop us to get inside. I don't know. It's not my level to discuss that. I was already inside. I wait for my soldiers. And until this time we also went out in the terrain, to try to learn the terrain and how we could use my unit down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, can you please tell us what type of briefings or training you received prior to the arrival of your company in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: You mean in Sweden before we ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In Sweden or anywhere else, the type of briefings and training that your unit or you, as the commander of that company, received.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Sweden, we have more or less a long tradition to be out in peace-keeping missions, so we have a lot of experience, officers and so on. So we was trained first week only with the officers in Stockholm in the middle of June. And after that, we trained, the whole battalion, each company and each garrison. And it was also with officers there who had experience to be out in peace-keeping missions. We also studying the background of the conflict, try to understand what is going on. I have experience of Cyprus before, since 1987, so I understand myself that it's very important to know the long history, hundreds of years' background. So I try to -- to read a lot of books to understand what is going on down there. And we also trained by the Danish in Denmark. They have experience from the Danish Battalion in Croatia. And we trained together with them, and they gave us their experience they have. And it was very -- some moment I don't really understand it, it could be so tough, but they have this experience. And when we came down to Bosnia, I was very happy that we have trained in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, can you describe for the Trial Chamber how the Nordic Battalion was structured.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We -- we start from the mechanised organisation, what you say an ordinary mechanised battalion in Sweden. That means there is one staff company, two mechanised company, and two tank companies, one artillery company, and one supply company. We couldn't use the tanks. We put them out. We put one more mechanised in -- company in. We put together the supply -- the staff and supply company. So that means we have staff and supply company, three mechanised company. And later, in the summer 1993 it was some agreement -- cooperation with Sweden and Denmark, so Denmark put in one tank company. And, of course, we also have a staff of about 50 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the approximate total manpower of NordBat in late 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I don't really understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many soldiers were in the Nordic Battalion in late 1993 approximately?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think it was about 800 soldiers. We was about 150 in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the name or numerical designator of the company that you commanded?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was 8 Mechanised Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did the 8th Mechanised Company remain in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: As I say, we arrived the beginning or the middle of October 1993, and we started a rotation in last week or something like this in March 1994, and it was right in the middle of April. So more or less six months in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what geographic area the Nordic Battalion patrolled or covered.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The battalion's area of responsibility was more or less the so-called Tuzla pocket. A little bit more. We also have Serbian areas to Zvornik in the east and even up in the north, but it was more or less the possibility for us to have some patrolling in the north. And we only do it when we have convoys, humanitarian convoys, and supply convoys from our own battalion in the east to Zvornik. In the south, it was down to the border to the British and Canadian Battalions. That means a little bit south of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the area of responsibility for the 8th Mechanised Company, the company that you personally commanded?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We have our company camp just outside Vares, and the area was from south -- south of, I think it was Dabravina or something like that, and up in north-west, the area of Ribnica, ending off west, north of Kladanj. And in south-east, what you could say east of Olovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us a few moments ago there were about 150 soldiers in your company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, the types of vehicles that your company had and the approximate quantity of vehicles that your company had.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I had three, what you could say, infantry platoons, and every platoon have three armoured personnel carriers, Swedish-built one. And they have 20-millimetres automatic cannon. And we also have a 4th platoon, with the same vehicle, three of them, and it was anti-tank missile platoon. I have one staff and supply platoon. They have some ordinary vehicles and also some -- and one medical APC on wheel. And I also have, from the staff and supply corps, I have the whole time a medical unit. So I had more or less six platoons. That means I have one staff and supply platoon, three infantry platoons, one anti-tank missile platoon, and one medic platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And these armoured personnel carrier that is your company had, were they tracked vehicles, or wheeled vehicles, or a combination?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The infantry and anti-tank missile platoon they had a tracked vehicle, APC 302, Swedish-built. And we also have, what I said, medical APCs. It was Finnish, on wheel. And we also have one more for the supply platoon and it was also with wheel, but it was also armed with heavy machine-gun. The medical APCs was unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, what colour were these vehicles that your company had?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: White with black "UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber the mission of the Nordic Battalion at the time your company, the 8th Mechanised Company, was in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Tuzla pocket was one of UN safe areas, and our mission was to support all humanitarian aid to this pocket. And that means, for my company, we have to the whole time have a road open from south of Tuzla -- sorry, south of Vares up to Tuzla. It was one -- more or less the only way up to this pocket. This was also one way from east, via Zvornik. But I think most of the humanitarian aid came from the south via Vares and north direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have told us, sir, that your unit was garrisoned near Vares. Can you please tell us precisely where your company was located and describe for us the camp where your unit was stationed.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Vares is a town within the valley, and the road is going through this town, and in the direction to Tuzla after Vares there is a tunnel, and after this tunnel there is a sawmill on the left side of the road where I have my camp. That means about -- not more, I think 7, 8 hundred metres from Tuzla -- I'm sorry, from Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe your camp briefly.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: When I arrived, it was a Canadian Engineering Company there, and they have tents outside. I understand that I'm going to be there in wintertime, so I don't want to be outside with my tent. So we negotiate with some owners of the sawmill down in Vares and we have possibility to put our tent inside the buildings. So where we put up our so-called camp, and used what you can say only the half part of the sawmill, more or less the factory where were built some furniture and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many of your platoons were garrisoned at the sawmill near Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: More or less all of the platoons was there, but as I say, they are not arrived. The first platoon arrived the 20th of October, and the last APCs and the last soldiers arrived in the beginning of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the period from the 20th of October, 1993, when the first platoon arrived, until mid-November 1993, how many of your platoons were in place?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I have all of my platoons there without three APCs from the anti-tank missile platoon. They arrived in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, sir, all of your platoons were garrisoned at the sawmill near Vares.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. They had -- this was, so to say, our camp. But I also used them to be out in the terrain for observation posts, checkpoints, and to patrolling, and that means that they sometimes was not back on the camp at night-time; they were out even at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what types of tasks - you've mentioned a few - what types of tasks your platoons were sent out to do within the first few days of your deployment in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I had been down there some weeks, and I understand -- I'd been informed too that it was something going on in Vares area. And when I was out in the terrain, I understand that it was a sensitive area and it was more or less some shooting in the west between the Bobovac Brigade and what I understand, the 3rd Corps, or the units from the 3rd Corps. I understand also that it was sensitive in this, what you could say, south-west part of the Bobovac Brigade area. There was two villages, Muslim villages. I think the name was Mijakovici and Dragovici, something like this. And I was a little bit afraid that the Bobovac Brigade should do anything wrong to these people in this village. And I visit them in those village one day, I think, in the beginning of October. And I understand that the situation there was not so good. They have not got a lot of food. And so I decided to, my first soldiers, to have them in a position up on the hill outside the village, the Croatian village with the name Kopjari. And the Bobovac Brigade, I think they also want me to be there because I was afraid to be attacked. But of course we -- our mission was not to take part in this war. And we -- it was very clear to my soldiers and to my officers that they shouldn't be close to the trenches and to the positions of the Bobovac Brigade's positions. And my missions was to observe down to the two Muslim villages so we could be there so they don't do anything wrong with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Colonel, let me briefly interrupt you. You have mentioned the Bobovac Brigade. Do you know to which army or military force the Bobovac Brigade was a constituent part?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I don't -- in this beginning, when I was down there, talked to the 2nd Corps up in Tuzla what was on the battalion level. But my battalion commander informed me that the commander of the 2nd Corps says to him that the Bobovac Brigade was a part of the 2nd Corps. If I asked the brigade commander if he was a part of 2nd Corps, he said, "No. I'm an independent unit in this area."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you've mentioned the 2nd Corps, and you also a few moments ago mentioned the 3rd Corps. To what army or military force were the 2nd Corps and 3rd Corps that you've mentioned --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After this meeting that you've told us about, did you subsequently determine what military force the Bobovac Brigade belonged to?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: What I can understand - I could also see it on the vehicles - it was HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, where was the Bobovac Brigade located or headquartered in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was in Sport Hotel, maybe 200 metres after my camp in direction to Tuzla. The left side was a Sport Hotel. And there they had the headquarter of this brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So this was in the vicinity, then, of Vares.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Sorry, it was ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the vicinity or region of Vares.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, it was the Vares area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From your location near Vares, where was the 2nd Corps of the BH army located?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: They had -- as I say, my company area was so-called also outside the Bobovac Brigade area. That means I also start immediately to negotiate with units from the 2nd Corps. That means I have contact with the brigade commander in Olovo. I also have some meetings with what you can say the command of the 3rd Operation Group in Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to which army did the 3rd Operation Group, located in Kladanj, belong to?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The 3rd Operation Group in Olovo belonged to the 2nd Corps in BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, I'm not sure -- the transcript doesn't reflect an answer to my previous question. But where was the 2nd Corps of the BH army located in relation to where your company was garrisoned in Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The 2nd Corps have -- the area of the 2nd Corps was more or less Tuzla pocket, and the headquarters was up in Tuzla. The units I have contact with from the 2nd Corps was the brigade in Olovo and the 3rd Operation Group in Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Colonel, from -- or in relation to where your unit was in Vares, where was the 3rd Corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army located?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: What I understand -- I don't really know it in this time, but I understand it later, some months later, that they have the headquarters in Zenica. And the border between -- like I say, the Bobovac Brigade from HVO, they had positions in west, from the north to the south in the village of Borovica and down to the village of Kopjari. West of these two villages, more or less, it was units from the 3rd BH army Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be correct, then, sir, based on what you've told us, that within the area of responsibility of your company the 2nd Corps and the 3rd Corps of the ABiH were both in that area?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, but it was most the 2nd Corps. I -- I don't really remember the border for my company, but I think it was more or less the same border between the 2nd -- sorry, the Bobovac Brigade and the 3rd Corps. Maybe I have little bit more. But I don't really remember exactly what the border was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, can you describe for us the situation on the ground towards the latter part of October 1993 with respect to these various military units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Well, beginning in -- when I arrived, the first I observed when I came to Vares, it was that there were a lot of refugees inside the city. And what I could understand and what I'd been informed about was that they have -- that it was, what you call, Croat people and they was escaped from the area of Kakanj and the surrounding areas from this area. Inside Vares area it was, what you say, Bobovac Brigade, meaning in my opinion it was not a brigade. It was smaller, but they call it a brigade. It was a mix between policemen, soldiers, and armed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was the situation from a military point of view calm, or was it tense, or was there actual fighting going on at the end of October 1993 in the vicinity of Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was -- when I arrived down there and before my platoon came down there on the 20th of October, it was small-arms shooting between, what you can say, the 3rd Corps units in west and the Bobovac Brigade, especially in the village of Kopjari and even in south. I think the name of the village was Planica or something like this. This means south-west or south of Vares. And they also informed us that they have wounded and dead soldiers there. And one day one of my officers and my medic officers was visit field hospital where they have transport with wounded Bobovac Brigade soldier, and this hospital was in 2nd Corps area, west of Kladanj in the Sport Hotel, and we was a little bit surprised about that because the Bobovac Brigade belonged to HVO. They was more or less fighting in west and south with BH army, but in north and east there was cooperation with -- to take care about wounded soldiers. And I also know that the brigade commander in Olovo, when I ask him about Bobovac Brigade, he informed me that they were talking together, they were never fighting. And I asked him about that, and he said that "We are friends. We are not fighting." "But they are fighting west," I said. And he said, "Yes, but that is the 3rd Corps. That is not the 2nd Corps. The 3rd corps, is more, so to say, angry or more hard line about this brigade than we are."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time in late October 1993 when the tensions dramatically increased in the vicinity of Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. After Kopjari, the 21st of October in the morning, the village of Kopjari was attacked. And I have -- my information before was it was not a surprise for me. I only was waiting when they should do it. And the attack was very successful for the BH army. They used infantry units to attack. They used also to -- we had a small attack, I think, in the direction of Borovica. But the big attack came from the small village near Mijakovici and Dragovici, up from the valley up to the hill. And everything was over for some hours. They also used the fog when they attacked. And in my opinion, they do it very well in a professional, military way. I have a unit there and they observed and report everything to me. And I arrived to the area about -- just before lunchtime. I was stopped in the checkpoint, temporary checkpoint from the BH army and stopped there. I was not allowed to enter the area. And it was maybe 1 or 2 kilometres from the village of Kopjari. I tried to negotiate to come up to the village. When I was out of my vehicle, it was heavy fighting up in the woods, on the right side of the valley. I could hear a lot of small arms and also grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me briefly interrupt you at this point. Do you know which unit or units were engaged in this small-arms fire that you heard at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. The defending was from -- the defender was Bobovac Brigade, HVO. And what I understand, later it was -- BH army have attacked and it was units from the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention, sir, towards the latter or the last few days of October 1993. Can you describe for us what the situation in the area of Vares was like in the last few days of October 1993.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. After Kopjari was taken over -- control of the BH army, it was -- it was some escalation down -- down in Vares. We observed new people or new soldiers there. And they don't -- we observed that that because they were more armed than ordinary HVO soldiers was in Vares. They have what you call, a cross in the ear, they have cross in the neck here, and they were very provocative towards us and towards civilians in Vares. So we understand that something is going on in Vares and it was not HVO soldiers from the area. They came out from some place in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you happen to know these people that you've described and who were very provocative, do you know to which side of the conflict they were affiliated?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: They were belonging to the HVO. It was what you can call HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you later become aware of what these soldiers were doing?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. The 23rd of October at the morning, I have one of my units drove up to the village of Kopjari to have some rotation of unit. They were stopped in Vares, north part of Vares, was not allowed to go up the road to -- to the direction Kopjari. I had one report from my military police was not allowed to -- had no freedom of movement in Vares. We have that before. So something was going on. So I immediately use my car to the Bobovac Brigade headquarters in the Sports Hotel and nobody there want to talk to me. Normally I have lots of -- I have good cooperation -- not cooperation -- good contact with them. But no commanders want to talk to me. And it was some staff officer there who could speak English and he said it was a bad day for the Bobovac Brigade, something was wrong. They had been attacked in the south. And the village they had been attacked was Mir -- Mir, you know, Mir which means "peace." That's very bad. They do that and that. And he also has informed me that they have attacked, in that case, the village of Stupni Do. And he explained therefore it was to have an open supply road. In the military view of that, I think it was nothing wrong about that. But the situation was I was not allowed to talk to them, I was not allowed to have freedom of movement. I was sitting there more or less the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, you just mentioned the village of Stupni Do and you told us that that village was attacked. Do you know which force attacked Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. It was forces from HVO. And when I was sitting there, I was observing because I had a view of the entrance to the hotel, that they arrived with some wounded HVO soldiers who was black in the face and ... and I understand that something was going on there. I also understanded that it was a -- it was a Muslim village. I don't know that before. And we tried to negotiate to have a possibility to visit this village, to look to and observe that they don't do anything wrong against the civilian people. But the answer was no because we have no commanders there and so on. And when I was sitting there, suddenly a group of men arrived. They say, "Now the men from Kiseljak has arrived." And in this group also was one man named -- Ivica Rajic, and he more or less took over the command in the Bobovac area when he is arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What -- to the best of your recollection, sir, what day or date did the attack on Stupni Do occur?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The attack started in the morning of 23rd of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me now take you to the 31st of October, 1993. Can you please describe for us the situation on the ground in the area around Vares on the last day of October 1993.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: But you mean the 21st of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The 31st of October, the last day of October.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The last day of October, it was -- a lot of village have been fallen around Vares. The BH army have also start attacked from the north. And I think the village of Borovica was taken by the 3rd Corps. And they also have started attack from south. I don't know if -- which name of the corps. I have heard of about 6th Corps and 1st Corps. So that was the situation. I mean, I think the HVO brigade in Vares was pressed more or less to the Vares area and in the east to the village of Dastansko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, how long did the Bobovac Brigade of the HVO remain in Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I don't really know when they start, but I think they take the command there in the summer 1993, sometime like this. And until they leave in the beginning of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe the circumstances, if you're aware of them, of the departure of the Bobovac Brigade from Vares in the beginning of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: They was to say -- there was civilians in the road between Olovo and Vares. They escape. It was very bad to look at that, civilians, old people. And so I tried -- I have information from my battalion commander in Tuzla. You can try to negotiate with the 2nd Corps, because we have some forward staff unit in -- I think the name was Rijeka or something like this, north of Vares. So I used an APC, some guards, and an interpreter, and get to the north. And I came to the front line, and it was no problem to take me through this. And I meet there deputy commander of 2nd Corps up in Rijeka. It was one civilian there. It was a mayor of Vares -- sorry, of Tuzla. Mayor of Tuzla. And it was also the commander of the 3rd Operational Group from Kladanj. We was talking about a situation. We was trying before to have some cease-fire in the area, both the BH army in Dabravina and now I try to do it up with this 2nd Corps. So they give me a letter. In that letter it was written about to the HVO in Bobovac Brigade that "you are a part of -- of 2nd Corps. Be our friends. Don't shoot, fight any more. And came up to have a meeting here tomorrow in Rijeka." Something like this was what was written in that letter. When I came back to Vares, it was dark, and I stopped my APC outside the Bobovac Brigade headquarters, the Sport Hotel. It was hundreds of civilians there. They was angry about me from the UN. It was maybe a little bit dangerous to leave APC, but I do it. And me and my interpreter, we walk up to the Sport Hotel. It was dark there. It was no electricity. They was burning papers, and I understand that they was ready to leave this headquarters. That was the situation that -- this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall the approximate day or date that this happened?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think it was the 2nd of November. And the next day, the 3rd of November, it was -- I have a report immediately at the morning at the Bobovac Brigade headquarter in the Sport Hotel that there was burning. It was more or less already destroyed, totally destroyed. And even also it was a lot of people, thousands of them, in Dastansko area who have escaped from Vares area and surrounding areas. We also have reporting from my units down in Vares and there was no more HVO soldier there. They have more or less leave the town. And so I -- I have decided the evening before to try to open the school, because we know that there was more than 200 Muslims men inside there and we was afraid they -- we know that they beat them up, but we was also afraid they should kill them. So I decided to lead an operation in the next morning in the daylight to broke up the school. And we do it, but it was no policemen there. It was no HVO soldier there. It was only these prisoners, Muslims men. And we find all of them, and some of them was beaten up, but they have not killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, you've told us that on the 3rd of November you had a report that the hotel was burning and that there were no more HVO soldiers in the town. Do you know why there were no more HVO soldiers or why the Sport Hotel was burning?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: What I understand, they burned the hotel because it was a headquarter. They don't want it to fall in the BH army's, so-called, hands. I also meet one man, a Croat man, who was burning his own house. And I asked him, "Why? Why do you burn such a beautiful house?" And he said, "I must leave, and I don't want it came to Muslims. It's my house. And it's only for my family." But this morning it was this house and it was another house just outside my camp also was burning. And it was some accident down in the hospital in Vares and it was a small firing even there, a small -- but that was all. And it -- when I was down in Vares this morning, the prisoners we have take out from the school, we could hear small, single shooting in the town, but that was all. I couldn't observe any soldiers. When I was later this morning up in the mayor house and inside this house to look after some paper, I heard two shots from the police station. It was on the opposite side of the square. And I sent immediately in soldier there is because I was afraid we had killed somebody there, but they only destroyed the television. But we also find one man -- old man there and he was very, very bad beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, on this day, that is, the 3rd of November, 1993, can you tell us whether or not there was any fighting in the city of Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what happened the following day, that is, 4 November 1993.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. We -- under these days we have a lot of international journalists. That means also from -- big journalists, BBC, Reuters, AP, and so on.
